thread.title: 3 Questions You Need To Answer Before Retiring

author: Colorado Wealth Management Fund
title: 3 Questions You Need To Answer Before Retiring
text:
This research report was produced by The REIT Forum with assistance from Big Dog Investments .
Investors who are planning to retire soon have some extra work to do.
They need to know the answers to a few key questions to ensure they don’t regret their decision.
Question 1: What will you do if you need to return to work? When an investor is nearing retirement, they need to consider the possibility of returning to the workforce at some point. Ideally, this is a backup plan that is thought out but never actually necessary.
Think of it like a seatbelt.
You should always wear your seatbelt inside a moving vehicle. However, you strongly hope that you won’t get in an accident. In the same manner, this plan should be something you have simply so you can feel more comfortable. In the event that it is actually needed, you would be very glad to have prepared the plan ahead of time.
Often, retirees are leaving a position with respectable pay and important duties. If they have not planned ahead, they could be forced to re-enter the workforce in a job with neither of those traits. This can be an advantage of working with a smaller employer. They may be willing to keep you in mind for future positions if you ever need to return. If you are friends with the owner and keep them informed about your situation, they can be a valuable resource. You’re helping them at the same time.
If you were to remain available on a part-time or very limited basis, you could remain tied in with the company, if that is something you desire. This can also be a great opportunity to be active and involved in retirement. If you hate your job or your employer, this would not be a desirable option.
Question 2: What will your income statement look like? A critical step of planning for retirement is designing the income statement. Many retirees have a significant reduction in their expenses after they retire. However, a few retirees find their expenses actually increase. You will need to determine which option makes sense for you.
To make the income statement work, retirees can focus on increasing revenue or decreasing expenses. If the investor is already retired, it is more difficult to create a meaningful increase in income without taking on an additional job. Being forced to take on that job is the opposite of retirement.
The key element here is choice. Being retired is all about choice. It doesn’t mean being able; it means having more freedom to choose what you will do.
Some investors believe they can increase income by simply purchasing higher yield securities. There is nothing wrong with pursuing a higher dividend yield, but it often comes with significant added risk. Many investors make the mistake of believing that as long as they do not sell the stock the risk is irrelevant. That is wrong.
When a company slashes the dividend to zero, the income investor still loses their source of income. Continuing to hold onto the shares will do nothing to replace the lost income. When the dividend is slashed to zero, the share price usually plunges dramatically as well, so the investor will have far less capital to reinvest.
Even when an extremely high dividend is sustained, it rarely grows. This can be a major challenge for investors because of inflation. If inflation picks up, we would expect a significant increase in interest rates. The exceptionally high yields often come from excessive leverage, which means the increase in interest rates will make things much harder for the company. Instead, I would suggest investors focus on stronger companies and use a few preferred shares to boost the overall yield of the portfolio.
Question 3: What will the balance sheet need to look like? The reason I address the balance sheet after the income statement is that investors should focus on the income they will need first and then design a balance sheet that can support it. Investors who look at the balance sheet first will often simply evaluate how much they have. They will look at the current savings and the income requirement and use that to determine the yield they will need. That often leads to buying sucker yields. It is more prudent to determine the income that will be necessary and a reasonable yield to expect. After that, work on how to build a portfolio large enough to support that income without gambling on sucker yields.

The above companies are proven dividend payers that have been tested with time. While some of them may not see exceptional growth moving forward, your dividend is more reliable.
At The REIT Forum, we focus on REITs (real estate investment trusts). They are the most convenient tool for owning a small piece of a real estate portfolio. For investors looking to get into real estate, REITs offer the benefit of diversification and a liquid market (publicly traded REITs) for buying and selling shares.
For instance, I’ve invested in many of the apartment REITs. The big 7 apartments REITs are AvalonBay Communities (NYSE: AVB ), Equity Residential (NYSE: EQR ), Essex Property Trust (NYSE: ESS ), Mid-America Apartment Communities (NYSE: MAA ), Camden Property Trust (NYSE: CPT ), UDR, Inc. (NYSE: UDR ), and Apartment Investment & Management Company (NYSE: AIV ). I do not consider any of these to be terrible REITs. They do differ in aggressiveness and which cities they are located in. Currently, AVB is very attractive. AVB is a great dividend growth stock to add to your portfolio today.
If investors ask themselves the 3 questions in this article, they should be better equipped to face retirement. Knowing these answers will also help with anything going awry after retirement.
